newsitem.title: UK: Crude oil recovers as heating oil demand picks up.
newsitem.headline: Crude oil recovers as heating oil demand picks up.

text.p: World oil prices firmed on Thursday as Germany came into the market to buy heating oil, which remained scarce enough to warrant a rise in the overall cost of the barrel of crude, dealers said.
"It seems that heating oil is the backbone of the market again," said Refco Energy Vice-President Victor Yu in New York.

World benchmark Brent Blend for December delivery closed at the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) in London at $22.25 a barrel, six cents up on the day, after rising to an intra-day high of $22.48
The market's main prop was again gas oil -- European heating oil, which is also traded on the IPE.
The December gas oil contract rose $5 a tonne on Thursday amid signs that Germany, the biggest heating oil market in Europe, was stocking up ahead of the peak winter demand season.

Demand for gas oil from the Far East market was another price prop on Thursday with shipping economics making it difficult to send any European surplus to the United States, where heating oil inventories are still below year-ago levels.
Brokers at the IPE said the market strategies of individual trading houses had introduced an extra level of volatility into gas oil futures, and had contributed to the day's price rises.

In the longer term, low heating oil stocks in the run-up to the peak northern hemisphere winter demand period were one of the main factors behind the blistering rally in oil to a six-year peak of $25.06 per barrel in mid-October.
But mild weather, a recovery in heating oil stocks and investment fund selling helped wipe over 10 percent off the price of a barrel of oil.
"Crude seems to be kicking and screaming as it follows heating oil up," said Ed Kevelson, director of refined products at Paribas Futures Inc.

Analysts said the market barely budged after remarks by Iraq's main chief negotiator with the United Nations that he did not expect any change in the U.S. position on the oil-for-food deal until January 1997 at the earliest.
In an interview with Reuters in Geneva, Ambassador Abdul Amir al-Anbari put the full blame on Washington for the delay in implementing the stalled humanitarian accord signed last May.

Under the deal, Iraq would be allowed to sell $2 billion in oil over six months to buy food and medicines. The market has already discounted the possibility of Iraqi oil exports resuming before next year.

The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) had factored in the estimated 700,000-800,000 barrels of Iraqi crude oil when it set its ceiling at 25.03 million barrels per day (bpd) to make way for Iraqi exports, which had been widely expected in the fourth quarter of this year.

A Reuter survey on Thursday showed OPEC production crept higher in October, once again overshooting its output ceiling. But analysts said a resilient oil price seemed to indicate that the group was far from producing too much for world markets.
The survey of oil analysts, industry sources and OPEC delegates showed the producer group pumped out 25.97 million bpd in October, up from 25.86 million bpd in September.

Quota violations by most of the 11 members meant that the cartel was nearly one million bpd over its ceiling as a prolonged oil price rally encouraged most of them to take advantage of strong pre-winter demand.

"The high price is probably encouraging higher production but one cannot really say there is overproduction since it is being absorbed," said veteran OPEC watcher Mehdi Varzi of Kleinwort Benson in London.
